title: Invisible Labors: The Past, Present, and Future of Media Technology and Work
description: Explores how media and communications technologies, ranging from the telegraph and early computers to social media platforms and artificial intelligence, have shaped the politics of work and workplace control. Introduces students to theories of race, gender, and work, as well as literature from science and technology studies, the history of technology, and labor studies.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory
description: Topics vary each year and may include such problems as the relation of film and other media to structuralism, semiotics, metaphor/metonymy, point of view, and the writings of Burch, Barthes, Metz, Heath, Bordwell, Willemen, Wollen.
prerequisites_raw: Film Studies 96; and 192A or 192B; and consent of instructor.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Japanese American Internment Media
description: Explores the role of visual and print media in the WWII incarceration of Japanese Americans through various historical and theoretical perspectives. Topics include the production and remediation of domestic wartime propaganda, race and representation, and public and private memory.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Media/Empire_Decolonization: From Nanook to #NoDAPL
description: Explores the imperial entailments and decolonizing potentials of various media and communication technologies. From the telegraph to the Internet, and from cinema to social media, we will consider how specific histories of colonial domination and decolonial struggle have shaped (and continue to shape) global media cultures.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Media and Globalization
description: This theory course explores medias constitutive role in our experiences of globalization. Topics include: accumulation of capital and forms of dispossession; borders and migration; flows and frictions; geographies of displacement; global media conglomerates and piracy; risk and securitization; resource extraction, the commons, and grassroots mobilization.

title: Media In/Through Iran
description: Explores how Iran's cultural, technological, and political landscape offers generative ways of studying media: their alternative histories, adaptive practices, and subversive circulations. Engaging with an eclectic range of Iranian objects and practices from the nineteenth century to the present, students examine the role of media in forming identity and negotiating power while considering the material conditions that transform communications technologies.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Media and Modeling
description: Do models shape the world or does the world shape our models? This class considers the creation, application, and ethical implications of models in domains ranging from computer graphics and machine learning to science and the environment, finance, and architecture.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory – Film & Media and Policing
description: This seminar investigates the relationship between police power and film and media from the late nineteenth century to the present. Students will analyze a range of media including, photography, silent cinema, American and international studio and independent features, avant-garde film, dash cam, body cam, and cell phone footage, and digital technologies that employ crime statistics and predictive policing. In addition to film and media theory, students will study theories of criminality, punishment, and abolition.

title: Sports, Media and Modernity
description: Explores the relationship between sport, media, and modernity through two critical lenses: first, how sport acts as a cultural apparatus mediating institutions, collective identities, and power structures of modern societies; second, how evolving media technologies (from print cultures to data-driven platforms) transform how sport is staged, performed, and experienced today. Thinking through the topics of colonialism, nationalism, race, gender, technology, and spectatorship, students examine how sport both expresses and structures the cultural dynamics of modern life.

title: Occult Media
description: In this seminar, we will contend with definitions of media and how they interface with the occult. Throughout the quarter, students will conduct archival research, learn about media archaeology, and discover occult media in its many forms, including horror films, online folklore, divination tools, Ouija boards, tabloid reports of the Satanic Panic, magic lantern shows, spiritualist and countercultural periodicals, optical toys, podcast episodes, popular music, religious technology like Scientology’s E-Meter, and more. Each student will be guided through a personalized archival research project that includes a trip to special collections at UCSB Library.

title: Race and/in AI
description: Critical work on artificial intelligence has, by now, revealed it as an intense tool of surveillance, policing, and racialization. This work has demonstrated the vastly unequal distributions of the political effects of race; however, this work has also demonstrated alternative practices, both current and speculative, with, alongside, and/or against AI. This course traces these diverse accounts of race and/in AI with the goal of answering the following three questions: What, when, and where is race in AI?

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Sound, Media, and Society
description: Builds conceptual and analytical tools for a critical understanding of sound, media, and auditory cultures. Special attention is paid to how social and historical factors inform sound media and how sound media, in turn, inform cultural perceptions and practices.
